record.paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
record.original_question: Why have hierarchical galaxy-formation models been unable to reproduce both the observed galaxy luminosity function and the zero-point of the Tully-Fisher relation when disk circular velocity is evaluated at the half-mass radius using realistic galaxy-size calculations, and does this failure come from approximations in size modelling or from a more fundamental shortcoming of the cold dark matter paradigm?

evidence.quote: To close this section, I would like to remind that a long standing problem for hierarchical models has been to match the zero-point of the Tully-Fisher relation (the observed correlation between the rotation speed and the luminosity of spiral disks [38]) while reproducing at the same time the observed luminosity function.

As discussed in Baugh [39], no model with a realistic calculation of galaxy size has been able to match the zero-point of the Tully-Fisher relation using the circular velocity of the disk measured at the half mass radius.
It remains unclear if this difficulty is related to some approximation in the size calculation, or if it is related to more fundamental shortcomings of the cold dark matter model.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider hierarchical galaxy-formation models in a cold dark matter (CDM) cosmology, in which dark-matter haloes form by gravitational collapse and merging, and baryons cool inside these haloes to form rotationally supported disk galaxies. For each model galaxy one computes (i) a luminosity L (from a star-formation and feedback prescription) and (ii) a disk circular velocity V_c evaluated at the disk half-mass radius R_{1/2}, where R_{1/2} is obtained from a realistic size calculation that accounts for the angular momentum of cooling gas, the gravitational contribution of the baryonic disk, and the (possibly adiabatically contracted) dark-matter halo.

Two empirical constraints must be matched simultaneously:
(a) the observed galaxy luminosity function Φ(L), i.e. the comoving number density of galaxies as a function of luminosity, and
(b) the zero-point of the Tully–Fisher relation, i.e. the observed linear correlation log L = a log V_c + b between the luminosity of spiral galaxies and the rotation speed of their disks, with empirically determined slope a and intercept b.

Question: Construct a hierarchical galaxy-formation model based on the CDM paradigm, with a physically realistic prescription for disk sizes, that simultaneously reproduces the observed luminosity function Φ(L) and the observed zero-point b of the Tully–Fisher relation when V_c is measured at R_{1/2}. Determine whether the persistent failure of existing such models to achieve this simultaneous match is attributable to approximations in the modelling of galaxy sizes (e.g., angular-momentum conservation assumptions, halo response to baryonic contraction, or the treatment of the disk mass profile), or whether it reflects a more fundamental inadequacy of the CDM paradigm itself (e.g., halo concentrations or inner density profiles being incompatible with observed disk dynamics).
artifact.status_search_result: The simultaneous matching of the galaxy luminosity function and the Tully–Fisher zero-point has been a longstanding tension in semi-analytic hierarchical models. Subsequent work (e.g. Dutton 2008/2012; refined GalICS dynamical rotation-curve recipes; abundance-matching analyses showing a non-monotonic v_rot–v_vir relation due to the stellar-to-halo-mass ratio) has shown the tension can be alleviated by combining lower stellar mass-to-light ratios, lower initial halo concentrations, and the absence of strong adiabatic halo contraction, suggesting the problem is largely related to baryonic/size-modelling assumptions rather than a fundamental failure of CDM. However, no fully consistent first-principles model has been universally accepted as resolving the issue.

status_evidence.title: The Tully-Fisher Zero Point Problem
status_evidence.snippet: Three solutions illustrated: low stellar mass-to-light ratios, low initial dark halo concentrations, and no halo contraction.
status_evidence.claim: The TF zero-point problem can be alleviated within CDM by adjusting baryonic and halo response assumptions, suggesting a size/baryon-modelling origin rather than a fundamental CDM failure.

status_evidence.title: Galaxy luminosity function and Tully-Fisher relation: reconciled through rotation-curve studies
status_evidence.snippet: The v_rot-v_vir relation can fully account for this seeming inconsistency due to the strong dependence of stellar-to-halo mass ratio on halo mass.
status_evidence.claim: Reconciliation of LF and TF achievable when the non-trivial mapping between disk rotation velocity and halo virial velocity is properly modelled.

status_evidence.title: The hierarchical build-up of the Tully–Fisher relation
status_evidence.snippet: Refined semi-analytic models with dynamical rotation-curve recipes improve the predicted Tully–Fisher relation.
status_evidence.claim: Improved size/rotation-curve modelling within hierarchical models brings predictions closer to the observed TF zero-point.
